claims.text: Single-phase solid-solution formation in noble-metal-based HEA nanoparticles is governed by the interplay between rapid thermal cycling and surface and atomic diffusion kinetics.
Fast heating provides insufficient time for atomic mixing.
Fast cooling kinetically freezes incompletely mixed states.
Kinetically frozen states favor phase separation, elemental segregation, and irregular particle morphology.
A controlled dwell at an intermediate or diffusion-active temperature enhances surface diffusion and atomic rearrangement.
Enhanced diffusion during the dwell produces a more homogeneous elemental distribution.
Enhanced diffusion and atomic rearrangement favor stabilization of an energetically favorable single-phase FCC structure.
Differences among elemental diffusion kinetics generate local composition fluctuations when redistribution time is insufficient.
Local composition fluctuations lead to phase separation or elemental segregation.
The dwell provides enough time for atomic-scale rearrangement and mixing to overcome initial kinetic barriers.
Overcoming the kinetic barriers drives the nanoparticles toward their thermodynamically preferred single-phase configuration.
Relative to rapid thermal cycling without a dwell, the dwell-treated nanoparticles will have more uniform elemental dispersion.
Relative to rapid thermal cycling without a dwell, the dwell-treated nanoparticles will have improved particle morphology.
Relative to rapid thermal cycling without a dwell, the dwell-treated nanoparticles will more consistently form a single FCC phase.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble-metal-based HEA nanoparticles targeting FCC structures under rapid-thermal-cycling synthesis conditions.
The effectiveness of the dwell may be limited in systems with substantially different melting behavior or intrinsic diffusion coefficients.
